title: Provider Briefs: Treating-Provider Intelligence for LOP Defense
riskiest_assumption: Defense lawyers will pay by card, out of firm overhead, for provider-level facts they cannot get from CaseMark, a general LLM or their bar network. This bundles two claims: the briefs contain facts the lawyer finds new and usable (public-only data may be too thin for young-patient LOP providers with few Medicare beneficiaries), and the lawyer rather than a carrier can actually buy them.

title: Blind Test Lab for Survey-Fraud Defenses
riskiest_assumption: A paying customer, meaning a challenger detection vendor or a mid-size supplier, will put real money on a labeled-traffic test report from an unknown lab before any end buyer demands such evidence. The seller-pays-referee flows are observed (Dynata to Neutronian, suppliers to CIRQ, P&G's ISO 20252 mandate), but there is no evidence anyone pays for an outcome test. This is the unresolved core of the fatal critique. Secondary risks are the trust cold start for a young founder with no credential, vendor disputes of results (the NSS Labs pattern), and MIT/CloudResearch or DQC commoditizing the benchmark.

title: Stranded-Loan Cure Desk (formerly Finish Crew)
riskiest_assumption: A non-captive holder of stranded pre-PTO loans (credit union, community bank, small servicer) will pay a third party by purchase order about $1,500 or more all-in per job (or a $5,000-plus triage fee) rather than defer payments, cancel and refund, refer the borrower to a local rescue installer, use staff, or use GreenLancer. No RFP, budget line, price or named paying lender has been found by the dossier or any of the three critics, and no fallback payer exists (homeowner-paid money is post-PTO O&M, not completion). All three critiques converge on this point.

title: Converter-Model Validation for AI Power Vendors (ERCOT-first)
riskiest_assumption: At least a handful of power-electronics vendors (not Eaton, Vertiv, Schneider or ON.energy) lack a workable path to converter model validation and will put real money behind a neutral third party: a paid review now and a stated $60k or more later. The alternatives for them are doing it in-house, buying from Keentel, EPE, ZEG, Electranix or Powertech, or waiting for ERCOT to relax the rule. If no vendor will pay a third party, nothing else matters.

title: Direct-Notice Desk for Cattle Lenders
riskiest_assumption: Ag lenders in direct-notice states will pay real money (about $2,000 up front, about $30 per borrower per year after) to close a notice gap that is cheap to close by hand and that they already choose not to close, because the obstacle is friction rather than a belief that the risk is negligible. If they skip a $30 filing because they judge the risk small, no price makes this a business.

title: Smoke Report Coverage Matrix
riskiest_assumption: That a policyholder-side law or coverage firm, or a PA, with live files will hand over client reports and actually pay about $95-$149 per file for a descriptive coverage matrix, instead of using a general LLM, Purdue's free review or their own CIH. Ranked by risk x importance, this is first, since nothing else matters if nobody pays. Extraction accuracy (testable in parallel and fixable), Purdue's launch timing (outside our control) and the closing window (known) come after it.

title: Exclusivity-Stage Data Audit for China-Origin Preclinical Assets
riskiest_assumption: A first- or second-time China in-licensor at exclusivity, with a named budget owner, will pay $35-45k to a vendor with no track record for a preclinical data audit. The alternative is relying on the sponsor, a banker, in-house generalists, or an established vendor. There is no direct willingness-to-pay evidence: no price list, RFP or budget line was found. A second gate is that a credentialed, FDA-experienced bilingual principal exists and will be named.

title: Scribe Screen: Non-PHI Scribe-Cohort Run-Rate Screen for Physician Acquisitions
riskiest_assumption: Someone with budget authority in a physician-practice acquisition will pay at least $4,500, as a separate line item, for a scribe-specific E/M run-rate screen, and the incumbent coding and QoE firms will buy or tolerate it rather than absorb it into their own scope. No buyer demand evidence exists today. The runner-up is that the staggered design supports a causal label on enough real targets, since many rollouts are group-wide.

title: Repo-Day Refund Desk (residual of the Auto Loan-End Event Exchange)
riskiest_assumption: A reachable group of lenders exists that (a) currently leaves repossession and charge-off add-on refunds unworked, (b) is not already served by LCT, Allied or F&I Sentinel, and (c) has a budget owner who will pay a new, unreferenced vendor a named price.

title: Operating Authority Memos for Data Center Lenders
riskiest_assumption: A person who controls spend or conditions on at least one live or upcoming PJM/ERCOT financing treats generator-hour exposure under non-emergency curtailment as a felt, priced credit question, and will request a quote of $12k or more or write it into a checklist. If it is only a footnote settled by "DOE 202(c) will cover it", there is no business. A secondary assumption is that Tier C survives legal scrutiny.

title: Cure Desk: Cash-Worker Evidence Kit for Health Centers (post-critique)
riskiest_assumption: For cash-paid patients holding a Nebraska work-requirement notice, the coverage loss comes from missing or insufficient proof that a third-party statement would fix. It does not come from non-response (about 960 of roughly 1,090 Nebraska losses were non-response), and it is not already fixed by the free route (state assistance, "any information you have," or a state worksheet). If caseworkers do not treat a third-party statement as better evidence, nothing downstream matters, including attester response, willingness to pay and channel.

title: Home Equity Assurance for Data Center Neighbors (refined, demoted to a watch item)
riskiest_assumption: Someone with authority and budget (a developer, a county, or the land-use counsel drafting the development agreement) will put a third-party-administered pay-on-sale value guarantee for a ring of 500+ homes into a real agreement, at a total fee of $100k+, instead of a buyout, bond, check or commissioned study. All three critiques converge on this, and public evidence already leans against it: zero guarantees in ten executed agreements, buyouts everywhere, no RFP or ordinance naming an administrator.
